1.note: The word **Maher Shalal Hash Baz** is the name of a boy. It means “the spoil hastens, the plunder speeds” or “hastening to the spoil, speeding to the plunder.” Isaiah expands on the meaning of this name in verse 4. So that your readers can appreciate this, you may with to explain the meaning of this name in a footnote.
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the name Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz]

3.note: Isaiah is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **I drew near to the prophetess**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [I slept with the prophetess]

4.q: כִּ֗י בְּ⁠טֶ֨רֶם֙ יֵדַ֣ע הַ⁠נַּ֔עַר קְרֹ֖א אָבִ֣⁠י וְ⁠אִמִּ֑⁠י יִשָּׂ֣א אֶת־חֵ֣יל דַּמֶּ֗שֶׂק וְ⁠אֵת֙ שְׁלַ֣ל שֹׁמְר֔וֹן לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
4.note: The word **before** indicates a temporal sequence in which the second event will happen before the first event has time to take place. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [one will carry away the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria to the face of the king of Assyria before the boy knows to call out ‘my father’ or ‘my mother]

4.q: בְּ⁠טֶ֨רֶם֙ יֵדַ֣ע הַ⁠נַּ֔עַר קְרֹ֖א אָבִ֣⁠י וְ⁠אִמִּ֑⁠י
4.note: Isaiah is using **before the boy knows to call out my father or my mother** as a common expression of the culture to mean “before the child is very old” or “within a very short time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the boy is old enough to speak]
The pronoun **one** refers to the king of Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Assyrian king will carry away]

Here, **the face of the king of Assyria** represents the presence of the king of Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the presence of the king of Assyria]

5.note: It might seem that to say both **added** and **again** would be to express extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could represent only one of these terms in your translation. The UST models one way to do that.

6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if his quiet provision for his people were **the waters of Shiloah, the ones going gently**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my quiet provision for my people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and people celebrate]

7.note: The term translated as **so therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [for this reason]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [know this]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against the people of Judah]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Assyrian army were **the waters of the River, mighty and many**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the mighty and vast Assyrian army]

Here, **his glory** represents the military splendor and power of the king of Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of his military might]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all that makes him great]
The pronoun **it** refers to the River, that is, the flood waters representing the Assyrian army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the River will go up]

8.q: וְ⁠חָלַ֤ף בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ שָׁטַ֣ף וְ⁠עָבַ֔ר עַד־צַוָּ֖אר יַגִּ֑יעַ
8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Assyrian invasion were flood waters that **sweep into Judah** and **overflow and pass through until it reaches the neck**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will come into Judah. It will advance throughout until it nearly overwhelms the whole land]

The pronoun **it** refers to the River, that is, the flood waters representing the Assyrian army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the flood waters will sweep]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Assyrian army were a bird with **wings** that spread out over the land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the spreading out of its army]
The pronoun **its** refers to the Assyrian army, spoken of as a bird or flood. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Assyrian army’s wings]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **fullness** and **breadth**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how wide is] or [as wide as]
The word **Immanuel** is the name of a man. It means “God is with us.”

The word **until** indicates a temporal endpoint for the action described. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [reaching as high as the neck] or [to the point that it reaches up to the neck]

9.q: רֹ֤עוּ עַמִּים֙ וָ⁠חֹ֔תּוּ וְ⁠הַֽאֲזִ֔ינוּ כֹּ֖ל מֶרְחַקֵּי־אָ֑רֶץ
9.note: Isaiah is speaking to the distant peoples who cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the futility of their opposition to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the distant nations. Alternate translation: [The peoples will shout, but they will shatter! And all the distant ones of the earth will shatter!]

Isaiah says **all of the distant ones of the earth** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [people in lands throughout the earth]

Isaiah is repeating the words **Gird yourselves and shatter!** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You may gird yourselves, but you will certainly shatter!]

Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He is commanding the nations to prepare for war, but he means that their preparations will be futile. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Even if you gird yourselves, you will shatter! Even if you gird yourselves, you will shatter!]

10.note: Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See how the UST models this.

The expression **it will be thwarted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will thwart it]

Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [devise your plan]
The pronoun **us** refers to the people of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for God is with his people]

11.note: Isaiah is using the word **For** to introduce the reason for what he has just said. Use a connecting word or phase in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [I say this because]

Here, **strength of hand** represents the power and authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with great power and authority]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the behavior of the people were a **way** or path that they were walking along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against following the practices of this people]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fear**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they fear]
The pronoun **its** refers to this people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the fear of this people]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and do not be afraid of what scares them]

13.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **fear** and **dread**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [shall be the one you fear and he shall be the one you dread]

14.note: Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between being a sanctuary for those who trust him and being a cause of stumbling for those who do not. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet he will be a stone]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were **a sanctuary** that protects those who trust in him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will protect those who trust in him]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were **a stone of tripping and a rock of stumbling**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but a cause of stumbling and falling]

The phrases **a stone of tripping** and **a rock of stumbling** mean basically the same thing. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [but a stone that causes people to trip and stumble]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **stone** that is characterized by causing **tripping** and a **rock** that is characterized by causing **stumbling**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express these ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [but a stone that people trip over and a rock that people stumble on]

Here, **houses** represents the people or family lines of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the two families of Israel]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were **a trap and a snare** for those who do not trust him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a cause of capture]

The terms **a trap** and **a snare** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a deadly trap]

The word translated as **sanctuary** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. However, the context seems to call for a negative term, and scholars have proposed that the original reading may have been “snare,” the same term that occurs later in the verse. They suggest that a scribe may have inadvertently added a consonant to this term, thinking that the more common word “sanctuary” was intended. If there is a major translation in your area and it says “snare,” you may want to use that reading. Alternate translation: [a snare, and a stone of]

15.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the spiritual ruin of the people was their physically **stumbling**, **falling**, and being **broken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And many will be brought to ruin because of them and be shattered and destroyed]

The pronoun **them** refers to the stone of tripping, the rock of stumbling, and the trap and snare mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [over that stone and rock]

The expression **be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and shatter]

The expressions **be snared** and **captured** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the trap will snare them and their enemies will capture them]

17.note: Here, **house** means all the people descended from Jacob. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Jacob** means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob. Alternate translation: [from the descendants of Jacob]
The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s withdrawal of favor were him **hiding his face**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who has withdrawn his favor from the house of Jacob]

18.note: The terms **signs** and **wonders** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [are for remarkable signs]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:7. Alternate translation: [Look]

19.note: The pronoun **they** refers to people in general who might advise consulting the dead. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [people say to you]

Isaiah is using the question form to assert that a people obviously should seek to their God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [a people should certainly seek to its God!]

Isaiah is using the question form to express the absurdity of seeking the dead on behalf of the living. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [People should not seek to the dead on behalf of the living!]

20.note: Isaiah is presenting a possible condition, that there will be no hope for those who do not speak according to this word. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Whoever does not speak according to this word]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if a lack of hope were the absence of **dawn**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no hope for him]
The pronoun **him** refers to whoever does not speak according to this word. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for such a person]

21.note: The pronoun **one** refers to a person among the people of Judah, while the pronoun **it** refers to the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And a person will pass through the land]

In this verse, the pronouns **he** and **his** refer to the person who passes through the land, mentioned earlier in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that person will become angry]

22.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **trouble** and **darkness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. See how you translated the similar expression in 5:30. Alternate translation: [dark and troubling things]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if judgment and hopelessness were **darkness** and **thick darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [trouble and despair, overwhelming anguish, and into deep hopelessness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **gloom** and **anguish**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [gloomy and painful]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **gloom** that is characterized by **anguish**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anguished gloom]

The expression **he will be driven away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is his enemies. Alternate translation: [his enemies will drive him away]
